lesson.title: Compare working and staged changes
lesson.summary: After the scenario above, what content would a commit of the current index record?
explanation: Git has separate places for your working edits and the next commit’s staged snapshot. Inspecting one does not automatically inspect the other.
Imagine note.txt was committed as Moon. You edit it to Sea and stage it, then edit it again to Sky without staging. The staged snapshot still says Sea.

```bash
git diff -- note.txt
git diff --cached -- note.txt
```

git diff compares working files with the index, so the first command shows Sea becoming Sky. --cached compares the index with HEAD, so the second shows Moon becoming Sea. -- separates options from the named path. These commands inspect changes; they do not stage or commit them.
Changed situation: After the scenario above, what content would a commit of the current index record?
The index contains Sea. The later Sky edit is still only in the working tree.

lesson.title: Ignored does not mean untracked
lesson.summary: A token was committed before .gitignore was added. Is the token now removed from history?
explanation: An ignore rule prevents matching untracked files from being included by ordinary add operations. It does not erase a file already recorded in Git history.
Suppose debug.log is already tracked. Adding debug.log to .gitignore does not make its future edits disappear from status. A file’s tracked status and its ignore match answer different questions.

```bash
git ls-files -- debug.log
git status --short
```

ls-files lists paths known to the index. A listed debug.log is tracked. status --short summarizes staged and unstaged changes. Inspect both before deciding whether a cleanup is appropriate. Do not use a secret file for this exercise.
Changed situation: A token was committed before .gitignore was added. Is the token now removed from history?
Ignore rules do not rewrite commits. A real exposed credential needs rotation and an appropriate history-remediation process.

lesson.title: Resolve a conflict by checking intent
lesson.summary: Why is deleting all conflict-marker lines alone insufficient?
explanation: A merge conflict means Git could not automatically combine some edits. Choosing one side without understanding both changes can discard useful work.
One branch changes a greeting to Hello, Mira. Another adds an exclamation mark. The intended combined result might be Hello, Mira! rather than either branch’s exact line.

```bash
git status
git diff
# Edit the conflicted file after reviewing both intentions.
git add greeting.txt
git diff --cached -- greeting.txt
```

status identifies unmerged paths. diff helps inspect the conflict. Editing removes conflict markers and constructs the intended content. add records the resolution in the index; it does not prove the result works. Run the relevant check before completing the merge. Practice only in a disposable repository.
Changed situation: Why is deleting all conflict-marker lines alone insufficient?
A syntactically clean file can still lose behavior. Review both intentions and verify the result.

lesson.title: Undo a shared change with a new commit
lesson.summary: After a successful ordinary revert, does the original commit vanish?
explanation: A revert records a new commit that undoes a previous commit’s changes. The original commit remains in history, which helps collaborators understand what happened.
Imagine a shared commit changed a button label from Save to Send by mistake. A revert can restore Save while recording an explicit correction after the mistaken commit.

```bash
git log --oneline -5
git show <chosen-commit>
git revert <chosen-commit>
```

Inspect the exact commit before replacing the placeholder. revert applies an inverse change and can encounter conflicts if later edits overlap. This is an optional disposable-repository walkthrough, not a command to run against current personal work. Reverting a merge has additional rules outside this lesson.

Revert preserves the original history and adds a correction. It is different from rewriting shared commits.

lesson.title: Reduce a bug to a minimal reproduction
lesson.summary: Removing a component makes the failure disappear. Is the smaller example ready to report as a reproduction?
explanation: A minimal reproduction is the smallest example you can find that still demonstrates the same failure. It makes the cause easier to isolate and the result easier for another person to verify.

A page with twenty components fails when an empty list is passed to total(). Remove unrelated rendering while keeping the empty-list call. If the failure disappears, restore the last removed dependency and continue carefully.

reduce without an initial value cannot choose a starting accumulator from an empty array. The function call is the trigger, [] is the boundary input, and the thrown error is the observed failure. Adding an initial 0 is a possible fix, but first preserve the failing example as a regression check.
Changed situation: Removing a component makes the failure disappear. Is the smaller example ready to report as a reproduction?
A useful reproduction preserves the observed failure. Size reduction is secondary to fidelity.

lesson.title: Know what a test double proves
lesson.summary: The fake captured one message. Which conclusion is supported?
explanation: A test double replaces a dependency with controlled behavior. It can isolate the code you are testing, but it cannot establish that the real dependency behaves the same way.
A fake mailer records a message in an array. A passing test can show that your function requested the right recipient and text. It cannot prove a real email was delivered.

send is a method on the fake object. push appends the supplied message to an in-memory array. length counts captured requests. There is no network operation, delivery receipt, inbox check, or production credential here.
Changed situation: The fake captured one message. Which conclusion is supported?
The evidence covers the fake interaction. A real integration requires separate, authorized verification.

lesson.title: Review a dependency update as a change
lesson.summary: The lockfile changed and installation succeeded. Is compatibility established?
explanation: A dependency update changes code your application relies on. A newer version number is not evidence that your application remains compatible.
Suppose a date library update changes invalid-input handling. Your happy-path date still formats correctly, but an empty value now throws. Include that boundary in the checks for the update.

The manifest expresses dependency requirements; the lockfile records a resolved dependency tree. Review their diff together, read relevant release notes, and test the behavior your application uses. This inspection command does not install or approve an update.

lesson.title: Keep a source and license inventory
lesson.summary: An asset has no identifiable license notice. What should the inventory say?
explanation: A dependency or asset inventory records what was included, where it came from, and which notices accompany it. A file’s presence in a public repository does not by itself establish permission to redistribute it.
For an icon, record its package name, version, source URL, and license file. For an original illustration, record that it was authored for the project. Keep those categories distinct.

Example inventory row: asset = navigation icons; package = the exact installed icon package; version = the resolved version; source = its upstream release; notice = the retained license path; review status = checked or unresolved.

The version identifies the reviewed material. The notice path makes attribution discoverable. The review status prevents an unresolved item from being described as cleared. An inventory supports review; it is not a legal opinion or a substitute for reading applicable terms.
Changed situation: An asset has no identifiable license notice. What should the inventory say?
Missing evidence is an unresolved provenance or license question, not proof of permission.

lesson.title: Connect a release to exact source
lesson.summary: The hosting service reports a different source commit than the one tested. What should happen?
explanation: A release receipt should identify the exact source that produced the deployed artifact. A successful build from one revision does not validate a later revision.
Imagine commit A passed checks, then commit B changed the code. Deploying B while citing A’s tests leaves a gap. Rebuild or rerun the relevant checks for B before claiming that evidence applies.

```bash
git rev-parse HEAD
git status --short
```

rev-parse HEAD returns the current commit ID. status reveals uncommitted changes that are not identified by that commit. A complete receipt also needs the built artifact and the hosting service’s confirmed version or deployment ID; a Git command alone cannot prove publication.
Changed situation: The hosting service reports a different source commit than the one tested. What should happen?
Evidence must match the published source. A mismatch needs investigation, not an assumption.

lesson.title: Name the four prediction outcomes
lesson.summary: A normal message is flagged as spam. With spam as positive, what is this?
explanation: For a yes-or-no classifier, compare its prediction with a known answer. A positive prediction means the model says yes; it does not mean the prediction is correct.

Suppose positive means spam. A spam message flagged as spam is a true positive. A normal message flagged as spam is a false positive. Spam allowed through is a false negative. A normal message allowed through is a true negative.
Worked example: four messages have known labels spam, normal, spam, normal. Predictions are spam, spam, normal, normal. Each of the four outcome categories contains one message.

Read true or false as whether the prediction matched the known answer. Read positive or negative as what was predicted. Changing which class means positive changes the labels, so state the convention first.
Changed situation: A normal message is flagged as spam. With spam as positive, what is this?
The positive prediction was wrong, so it is a false positive.

lesson.title: Ask how many positive predictions were right
lesson.summary: A model flags four items and three are truly positive. What is its precision?
explanation: Precision asks: among the examples predicted positive, how many really were positive? It is useful when acting on a false alarm has a cost.
If a filter flags ten messages as spam and eight are actually spam, eight of its ten positive predictions were correct. Its precision on that set is 8/10, or 80%.

Worked example: filter A flags five messages, all spam. Filter B flags ten messages, eight spam. A has 100% precision and B has 80% precision on these predictions. This comparison alone says nothing about how much spam either filter missed.

The denominator is true positives plus false positives: every positive prediction. False negatives are not in that denominator. If there are no positive predictions, the raw ratio is undefined; evaluation tools must state their chosen handling.
Changed situation: A model flags four items and three are truly positive. What is its precision?
Precision uses the positive predictions as its denominator, so the ratio is 3/4.

lesson.title: Ask how many actual positives were found
lesson.summary: There are twelve actual positives and nine are found. What is recall?

lesson.title: Separate a score from a decision threshold
lesson.summary: The threshold rises while every score stays fixed. Did the model necessarily retrain?
explanation: A classifier may output a score before the application makes a yes-or-no decision. A threshold converts that score into an action under an explicit rule.
Suppose the rule is predict positive when score is at least 0.6. Scores 0.4 and 0.59 are negative; 0.6 and 0.8 are positive. The equality rule matters at the boundary.
Worked example: with unchanged scores 0.4, 0.6, and 0.8, raising the threshold from 0.5 to 0.7 reduces positive predictions from two to one. No model weights changed in this comparison.

A threshold changes which cases receive a positive decision. To assess the consequences, compare against known labels and count false positives and false negatives. A score is not automatically a well-calibrated probability.
Changed situation: The threshold rises while every score stays fixed. Did the model necessarily retrain?
The same model scores can be interpreted using a different decision threshold.

lesson.title: Keep evaluation information out of preprocessing
lesson.summary: Should a held-out test value help determine the training normalization mean?
explanation: Data leakage occurs when evaluation information influences training or model selection in a way that would not be available for a genuinely new case.

Suppose you standardize a numeric feature by subtracting its mean. Learn that mean from the training split, then apply the same value to validation and test cases. Computing it from the whole dataset lets held-out data influence preparation.

Worked example: training values are 2 and 4, so the training mean is 3. A held-out value 100 is transformed using 3. Recomputing the mean with 100 would change the transformation using evaluation information.

Fit preprocessing on training data inside each evaluation split. Transform held-out data using the fitted preprocessing. Similar leakage can occur through duplicate examples or information recorded after the prediction time.
Changed situation: Should a held-out test value help determine the training normalization mean?
The held-out set is meant to measure generalization. Its information must not shape fitted preprocessing.

lesson.title: Watch for a changed input population
lesson.summary: New users submit a document type absent from evaluation. What is the sound next step?
explanation: A model evaluated on one population may encounter different inputs later. Distribution shift means the data or its relationship to the target has changed.
A document classifier trained on short English notes may receive long multilingual scans after release. Its old evaluation result does not establish performance on those new inputs.

Worked example: the original evaluation has 100 typed notes and no scanned pages. A later batch is mostly scans. Measure performance on a labeled sample of the new cases before assuming the old result transfers.

Monitor meaningful input and outcome changes, then investigate whether evaluation data still represents actual use. A change in inputs is a signal to examine, not automatic proof that every prediction is wrong.
Changed situation: New users submit a document type absent from evaluation. What is the sound next step?
New evidence should address the changed population. Neither blanket confidence nor blanket failure follows from the old score.

lesson.title: Check retrieval relevance before trusting an answer
lesson.summary: The top-ranked passage is from an outdated policy. What should the application do?
explanation: Retrieval supplies candidate evidence to a model. A high similarity ranking does not guarantee that a passage answers the user’s actual question.
A user asks about the current refund policy. A retrieved page discusses a similar product’s expired policy. The words may be similar while the authority, product, and date are wrong.

Worked example: candidate A mentions refunds but is for a different product. Candidate B is the current policy for the requested product and covers the relevant situation. Check those facts before choosing which passage supports the answer.

Separate retrieval evaluation from answer evaluation. First ask whether the needed evidence was retrieved. Then ask whether the answer accurately uses it, states its limits, and avoids unsupported additions.
Changed situation: The top-ranked passage is from an outdated policy. What should the application do?
Ranking is a retrieval signal. Evidence still needs to match the question’s subject, timing, and authority.

lesson.title: Keep a regression set for model changes
lesson.summary: Two revisions have the same total pass count. Can you conclude they behave identically?
explanation: A regression set is a collection of representative cases used again after a change. It helps detect when an improvement in one area breaks behavior elsewhere.
Suppose a prompt change improves short summaries but starts omitting dates. Keep ordinary summaries, date-sensitive summaries, and previously failing cases in the evaluation set.

Worked example: revision A passes 18 of 20 fixed cases. Revision B also passes 18, but fails two different important cases. Equal totals do not mean equal behavior; compare the individual results and their consequences.

Record the input, expected criteria, model or prompt version, and actual outcome. Keep separate held-out cases so repeated tuning on the regression set does not become the only measure of generalization. No finite set proves universal correctness.
Changed situation: Two revisions have the same total pass count. Can you conclude they behave identically?
The same count can conceal different failures. Case-level evidence and failure importance matter.
